name: Corona Wastes
specific_features: Sand that glows faintly during stellar coronal mass ejections
description: Corona Wastes is a desert world baked beneath an active star prone to frequent coronal mass ejections. The silicon-rich sand that covers most of the surface responds to these solar events with a faint phosphorescent glow, transforming the nightside into a landscape of softly luminous dunes during periods of stellar activity. Wind-carved sandstone arches span canyon mouths where ancient rivers once flowed, their delicate forms testament to billions of years of patient erosion.

The thin atmosphere provides little protection from the stellar radiation, and surface temperatures swing dramatically between scorching days and frigid nights. The air is dry beyond measurement, with humidity approaching absolute zero in the deep desert regions. During coronal mass ejections, the atmosphere develops a faint shimmer as charged particles interact with trace gases, and the glowing sand turns the landscape into something between dream and desolation.

Desert flora has adapted to the extreme conditions by developing deep root systems that tap aquifers hundreds of meters below the surface and radiation-resistant cellular structures that actually metabolize some of the stellar particle bombardment. These plants are sparse but ancient, individual specimens estimated to be tens of thousands of years old. Their slow metabolism and extreme longevity make them living records of the planet's climatic history.

Corona Wastes has drawn interest from solar energy companies seeking to exploit the intense stellar radiation, and from botanists studying the radiation-metabolizing flora. The glowing sand phenomenon is still poorly understood but has potential applications in passive lighting and radiation detection. A small research settlement operates in the deepest canyon system, where the rock walls provide natural radiation shielding.
